title: Atahualpa's Ransom at Cajamarca
text:
In November 1532 Francisco Pizarro led about 170 Spaniards into the Andean town of Cajamarca. Atahualpa, the Inca ruler, was camped nearby with a huge army, fresh from victory in a civil war against his brother Huascar. He knew the strangers were few and seems to have regarded them as a curiosity rather than a threat. He agreed to meet Pizarro in the town square.

The Spaniards hid their horsemen, foot soldiers and small cannon in the buildings around the square. Late on 16 November Atahualpa arrived, carried on a litter and accompanied by thousands of attendants who were largely unarmed. According to the accounts of Pizarro's secretary Francisco de Xerez and his cousin Pedro Pizarro, the friar Vicente de Valverde approached with a breviary or Bible and demanded that Atahualpa submit to the Christian faith and the Spanish king. Atahualpa examined the book and threw it to the ground. At a signal the Spaniards opened fire and charged. In the panic, thousands of Inca attendants were killed, and Pizarro seized Atahualpa himself.

From captivity Atahualpa offered a ransom: to fill a large room once with gold and twice with silver. The Spaniards accepted, and over the following months treasure poured in from across the empire and was melted down. But once the ransom was gathered, Pizarro's men, fearing a rescue attempt, put Atahualpa on trial and executed him in July 1533. The leaderless empire was then conquered piece by piece.
lesson: Never let contempt for a weaker party lower your guard, and do not hand your fate to someone who has already shown he will betray you. A promise from a captor is not security.
people: Francisco Pizarro, Atahualpa, Vicente de Valverde
source: Francisco de Xerez, True Account of the Conquest of Peru (1534); Pedro Pizarro, Relation of the Discovery and Conquest of the Kingdoms of Peru (1571)
